paper.title: Association between intimate partner violence and birth outcomes among pregnant women in the STOP-VIO-PREG cohort: A cohort study utilizing Patient-Reported Outcome and Danish registers data
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 1740), verbatim: "Access to the PROdata is available through a collaborative agreement and granted access with Statistics Denmark and the Danish Health Data Authorities. …

variables_mentioned: gestational age at birth (time of birth)

registers.name_in_paper: the National Register of Patients / the National Patient Register of Diagnoses (Danish Health Data Authority)

linkages: PROdata linked to the Danish registers via the unique Civil Personal Registration (CPR) number, encrypted to identification numbers so that personal information remained anonymous
Mother-offspring pairs formed by linking each PROdata respondent to her registered offspring's birth record in the Danish Medical Birth Registry
In early 2023 the dataset was enriched with Statistics Denmark data and with National Register of Patients data from the Danish Health Data Authority

sample.universe: Pregnant women attending antenatal care at one of six participating hospitals (Odense University Hospital, Lillebaelt Hospital, Esbjerg Hospital, Hospital Soenderjylland, Copenhagen University Hospital, Hvidovre Hospital) in two of Denmark's five regions, screened with the PROdata questionnaire
selection_rules: By January 2023, data from all sites (n = 31 700) were merged
Excluded duplicates (individuals with multiple PROdata answers or pregnancies, n = 3003)
Excluded women with no registered offspring (n = 1194)
Excluded mothers who did not respond to the IPV questions (n = 4358)
Resulting in a total study population of 22 799 mother-offspring pairs (Figure 1)
sample.period: Data collected between November 2019 and September 2022 (Copenhagen University Hospital from November 2019, Region of Southern Denmark from January 2021, Hvidovre Hospital from September 2021); the cohort was followed until June 2023, when the last woman gave birth
sample.n_individuals: 22 799 mothers (28 697 pregnant women screened with PROdata; 27 157 with valid data; 22 799 responded to the IPV screening questions, a response rate of 83.95%)

construction_notes: Self-reported IPV defined by affirmative responses to one or more of the five DK-AAS items, referred to as 'screening positive' for IPV

Six IPV exposure definitions analysed: screening positive / ever IPV; any IPV within the last 12 months; ever physical IPV; physical IPV within the last 12 months; emotional IPV within the last 12 months; sexual IPV within the last 12 months
At Copenhagen University Hospital the DK-AAS sub-question asking 'by whom' was not incorporated alongside the main question

Time of birth categorized following WHO: extremely preterm (<28 weeks), very preterm (28-31+6 weeks), moderate or late preterm (32-36+6 weeks); term and late term following the Defining 'term' Pregnancy Workgroup: early term and term (37-40+6 weeks), late term and post-term (>=41+0 weeks)
PTB analysed as a binary variable: gestational age <37 weeks versus >=37 weeks
Birthweight categorized as LBW (<2500 grams), normal weight (2500-4000 grams), high birthweight (>4000 grams); LBW analysed as a binary variable: birthweight <2500 grams (no versus yes)
SGA calculated (no versus yes) with the formula published by Marsal: below the 10th percentile of the sex-specific ultrasound estimated curves for normal intrauterine growth
Highest completed level of education constructed using the international standard classification of education (ISCED 2011)
Preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and psychiatric/neurological conditions defined from ICD-10 codes in the National Patient Register of Diagnoses
Covariates selected a priori from subject-matter expertise and Directed Acyclic Graphs (Figure S1); PTB added to the adjustment model for the IPV-LBW association to estimate the direct effect
All statistical analyses conducted using STATA version 18
Tables 2 and 3 print per-outcome totals summing to 27 157 rather than to the 22 799-pair analytic sample; the risk ratios are transcribed as printed and the discrepancy is flagged per claim

key_assumptions.assumption: No adjustment is made: the reported risk ratio is the crude (unadjusted) association between the IPV measure and the birth outcome, so any causal reading additionally requires that the exposed and unexposed groups do not differ in determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper labels these estimates crude associations; Table 1 documents that women reporting IPV differ significantly on education, income, occupation, marital status, smoking and psychiatric disorders (all p < 0.001).

key_assumptions.assumption: The self-reported DK-AAS classifies IPV exposure without differential misclassification with respect to the birth outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state the AAS has high sensitivity and specificity, was translated and adapted following best practice and pilot-tested with 30 pregnant women, but also concede underreporting, information bias, and that the tool misses stalking and digital violence and only detects violence women are aware of.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the analytic sample on responding to the PROdata IPV questions and on having a registered singleton offspring does not bias the IPV-birth outcome association.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors report an 83.95% response rate and argue register data minimise selection and non-response bias, while conceding that disclosure barriers 'may introduce the potential for selection bias'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Temporal ordering: IPV is screened in the first trimester and the birth outcome occurs at the end of the same pregnancy, so the association cannot run from the birth outcome back to the reported exposure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The prospective design: PROdata is submitted before the first antenatal visit and the cohort is followed to childbirth. No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede an unmeasured common cause: potential underlying confounders linked to IPV such as poverty, unstable housing and reduced social support may contribute to the association found.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion, p. 1739; conceded rather than tested. The authors also acknowledge the limitations of observational studies in drawing causal conclusions.
